title: CORS, cookies, and httptest
summary: CORS is the server telling browsers which other origins may read its responses; it stops no request. Cookies carry sessions, so they need HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite and CSRF protection. httptest runs all of it in tests without a network.

examples.title: A CORS middleware: preflights, an allow-list, and what it doesn't stop

annotations.note: The key fact about CORS: the server only labels responses. The browser decides whether the page's JavaScript may read them. curl, Go programs and attackers' scripts ignore the labels entirely.

Reflect the request's Origin only when it is on the list, and add Vary: Origin so a cache never serves one origin's permission to another. "*" also works, but never together with cookies or other credentials.

A preflight is an OPTIONS request with Access-Control-Request-Method. The browser sends one before a PUT, a DELETE, or a POST with Content-Type: application/json, and sends the real request only if the answer allows it. Max-Age lets the browser cache that answer.
CORS wraps the mux, not the route. The mux only knows "PUT /notes/{id}", so a preflight reaching it would get 405 and the browser would never send the PUT.
For the other site the preflight succeeds as an HTTP exchange but carries no permission, so a browser stops there. A non-browser client simply sends the PUT, and the handler runs.

A sandboxed iframe without allow-same-origin has an opaque origin, sent as the string "null". StackLab's TS runner iframe is exactly that. Never allow-list "null": every sandboxed iframe, data: URL and file: page in the world has that same origin.
Three executions, not one: the handler ran for every PUT. Protect state-changing endpoints with authentication and CSRF defenses; CORS only protects the response from being read.

examples.title: Session cookies, non-ASCII values, and CSRF protection (Go 1.25)

annotations.note: The usual session cookie. The value is a random ID pointing at server-side state, so the cookie carries nothing worth reading. SameSite=Lax withholds it from cross-site POSTs and subrequests but keeps it on ordinary links into your site.
The __Host- prefix is a promise browsers enforce: such a cookie is rejected unless it is Secure, has Path=/ and no Domain, so a sibling subdomain can't set or overwrite it.

Cookie values allow only a subset of ASCII. net/http drops the bytes of ş and logs a warning on stderr; the log even shows the first byte as Å, UTF-8 read as Latin-1. Encode such values (base64url, or percent-encoding) and decode them on the way back.
Deleting a cookie is setting it again with the same name, path and domain and an expiry in the past. In Go, MaxAge < 0 sends Max-Age=0.

CrossOriginProtection rejects every method except GET, HEAD and OPTIONS when a browser sends it from another origin, judged by Sec-Fetch-Site or, failing that, Origin versus Host. Requests without either header (curl, server to server) pass, so it complements authentication.
srv.Client() trusts the TLS test certificate; a cookiejar makes the client keep and resend cookies like a browser, Secure ones included, because the server speaks HTTPS.
A browser sets Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site when another site's form posts here. The 403 means the logout never happened: the next /me still finds the session.

examples.title: Testing handlers with ResponseRecorder and NewTestServer (Go 1.27)

annotations.note: The fastest handler test: build a request with httptest.NewRequest, call ServeHTTP with a ResponseRecorder, inspect the result. The whole router runs, 405 included, with no socket and no goroutine. The CORS middleware from example 1 is tested the same way: set Origin on the request and check Access-Control-Allow-Origin in the result.

httptest.NewRequest builds a server-side request (Host example.com unless the target is absolute) and panics on bad input, which is what you want in a test. http.NewRequest builds a client request instead.

rec.Header() is the live map a handler mutates; rec.Result().Header is a snapshot of what was sent at the first write. Assert on the snapshot, or a header set too late will look correct. http.Error sets text/plain itself, which is why the error rows expect it.

NewTestServer (Go 1.27) runs a real server and client over an in-memory network: any host name reaches it, no port is opened, and t.Cleanup shuts it down. It also fails the test if a handler panics. httptest.NewServer is the loopback alternative when a test needs a real address.

use_cases: An API used by a browser app on another origin, such as a Vite dev server on :5173 calling a backend on :8080 without a proxy
Cookie-based sessions for server-rendered pages and same-site SPAs
CSRF protection for any cookie-authenticated endpoint that changes state
Handler, middleware and router tests that run in milliseconds without ports
strengths: CORS is a few headers in one middleware; no framework configuration DSL like Spring's CorsConfiguration
http.CrossOriginProtection (Go 1.25) gives token-free CSRF protection in one wrapper, unlike Django's or Spring Security's synchronizer tokens
http.Cookie models every attribute (SameSite, Partitioned since Go 1.23) and SetCookie validates what it writes
httptest covers three levels, recorder, in-memory server and loopback server, all in the standard library, where Java needs MockMvc or a test container
weaknesses: CORS mistakes fail silently on the server: the request succeeds, only the browser console complains
Invalid cookie bytes are dropped with a log line, not an error; nothing stops a deploy
CrossOriginProtection relies on headers that only browsers send, so it is a browser-facing defense, not authentication
A ResponseRecorder skips the transport: connection handling, Flush and Hijack behavior need a test server

pitfalls.title: Allowing the null origin
pitfalls.detail: Access-Control-Allow-Origin: null admits every sandboxed iframe, data: URL and file: document, including hostile ones. Serve such clients through a proxy or a data: URL design instead.

pitfalls.title: Reflecting any Origin with credentials
pitfalls.detail: Echoing whatever Origin arrives plus Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true lets every website read authenticated responses. Compare against an explicit allow-list.

pitfalls.title: CORS middleware inside the router
pitfalls.detail: With method patterns, OPTIONS reaches no route and the mux answers 405, so every preflighted request fails. Wrap the mux.

pitfalls.title: Treating CORS as access control
pitfalls.detail: Simple requests, such as a form POST, are sent cross-origin without any preflight, and non-browser clients ignore CORS entirely. Authenticate, and protect cookie-based state changes against CSRF.

pitfalls.title: Non-ASCII in cookie values
pitfalls.detail: "Ayşe" becomes "Aye" with only a log line to show for it. Base64url- or percent-encode the value.

quiz.q: A page on https://evil.example calls fetch("https://api.example/notes/1", {method: "PUT"}). Your server answers the preflight without Access-Control-Allow-Origin. What happens?
options: The PUT is sent and its response hidden
The browser never sends the PUT
The PUT is sent without cookies
quiz.why: PUT is not a simple method, so the browser preflights first and stops when the preflight grants nothing.

quiz.q: Why does a sandboxed iframe (sandbox="allow-scripts", no allow-same-origin) send Origin: null?
options: Its document gets an opaque origin, which serializes as null
quiz.why: Without allow-same-origin the sandbox gives the document a unique opaque origin, and opaque origins serialize as "null".

quiz.q: http.SetCookie(w, &http.Cookie{Name: "n", Value: "Ayşe"}). What reaches the browser?
options: n=Aye, with a warning logged by net/http
quiz.why: Cookie values are limited to a subset of ASCII; net/http drops the invalid bytes and logs, so encode non-ASCII values.

quiz.q: What does an httptest.ResponseRecorder test not exercise?
options: The real HTTP transport: connections, serialization, Flush and Hijack
quiz.why: ServeHTTP is called directly with a recorder, so routing and middleware run, but no connection or wire format is involved; use a test server for those.

body:
## Concept

An **origin** is scheme + host + port: `http://127.0.0.1:5173` (Vite) and
`http://127.0.0.1:8080` (the Go backend) are different origins. Browsers let a page *send*
many cross-origin requests (links, forms, images, simple fetches) but not *read* the
responses, unless the server opts in with CORS headers:

- **Simple requests** (GET, HEAD, POST with a form or plain-text body) are sent directly;
  the browser shows the response to the page only if `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` matches.
- **Preflighted requests** (PUT, DELETE, JSON bodies, custom headers) start with an
  `OPTIONS` request; the real one follows only if the preflight answer allows it.
- With cookies (`credentials: "include"`), the server must name the exact origin and send
  `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`; `*` is rejected.

The `Origin` header is the string `null` for **opaque origins**: documents in an
`<iframe sandbox>` without `allow-same-origin`, `data:` and `file:` documents, and requests
after cross-origin redirects.

**Cookies** carry sessions automatically, which is both their convenience and their
danger. `HttpOnly` hides them from scripts, `Secure` keeps them off plain HTTP, `SameSite`
limits cross-site sending, and the `__Host-` prefix pins them to one host. Because the
browser attaches them to requests other sites trigger, cookie-authenticated state changes
need **CSRF** protection; since Go 1.25 that is `http.CrossOriginProtection`.

**httptest** tests all of this without a network: `NewRecorder` and `NewRequest` call a
handler directly, `NewTestServer` (Go 1.27) runs a real client and server over an in-memory
network, and `NewServer`/`NewTLSServer` listen on loopback.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **JS/React**: you have met CORS as a red console error. This is the other side: the
  server's headers decide, and the browser enforces. The Express `cors` package is the same
  middleware as example 1.
- **Java/Spring**: `@CrossOrigin` and `CorsConfiguration` generate these headers; Spring
  Security's CSRF tokens solve what `CrossOriginProtection` solves with `Sec-Fetch-Site`.
  `MockMvc` corresponds to the `ResponseRecorder` style, a random-port `@SpringBootTest` to
  `httptest.NewServer`.
- **Python**: Django's CSRF middleware uses tokens; `flask-cors` and Starlette's
  `CORSMiddleware` add the headers. Flask's `test_client()` calls the app without a socket,
  like a recorder.
- **C/C++**: a non-browser client never sees CORS at all, which is the point to remember.

## How it works

StackLab's TS runner, `src/features/runner/browserTs.ts`, is a worked example of the
null origin:

    <iframe sandbox="allow-scripts" srcdoc="...lesson...">
      - no allow-same-origin   -> opaque origin, Origin: null, no access to the app's
                                  DOM, storage or cookies
      - CSP default-src 'none' -> no fetch at all, so lessons stay deterministic
      - libraries              -> data: URLs in an import map (ADR-0010), which need
                                  neither CORS nor a CSP exception

The app itself avoids CORS too: the Vite dev server proxies `/api` to the backend, so the
browser only ever talks to one origin, and the backend sends no CORS headers at all. If a
lesson iframe were allowed to call the API, the backend would have to allow `null`, which
would also allow every other sandboxed document on the web.

## Design notes

Avoid CORS when you can: serve the frontend and the API from one origin, in development
through a proxy as StackLab does, in production behind one reverse proxy. When you need
it, keep an explicit allow-list, reflect only listed origins, add `Vary: Origin`, answer
preflights before routing, and keep `Allow-Credentials` off unless the client sends
cookies.

For sessions, store a random ID in a `__Host-` cookie with `HttpOnly`, `Secure` and
`SameSite=Lax`, keep the data on the server, and wrap state-changing routes in
`CrossOriginProtection`. Generate IDs with `crypto/rand.Text`. Keep tokens for third-party
API clients in the `Authorization` header instead: no cookies, no CSRF, but the client has
to store the token somewhere scripts can reach.

Test at the cheapest level that covers the behavior: recorder tests for routing,
validation, status codes and headers; `NewTestServer` when the client side matters
(cookies in a jar, redirects, TLS); loopback servers only for code that needs a real
address. Lesson go.testing.fakes-httptest goes further with fakes and golden files.
